summary:
Have you ever wondered which place on Earth looks most like a crater on the Moon or a plain on Mars? That’s the question behind Analog Atlas.

Pick a region on our 3D globe and we describe it with 24 specific features, from slope and thermal inertia to ice and minerals. We then score Earth with a Similarity Index from 0 to 100, tuned for landing, resource, habitat or science missions.

First we test ourselves: for 19 of 20 cases, the analog scientists already trust lands in our top five; random picks manage about 31%. Jezero Crater’s best match is Lake Salda in Türkiye, the site the Mars 2020 team studied. Then we scan 58,289 land cells worldwide, built from NASA and other satellite data in Google Earth Engine, to suggest new sites.

We found that 19 of 22 NASA-involved analog campaigns took place in high-income countries. So Analog Atlas gives the Global South a priority, never a filter.

Every result is honest: each card shows where the analogy breaks, and gravity, radiation and day length are shown but never scored. Our mineral layers are rough proxies, and we say so in the app.
details:
Analog Atlas is a similarity tool. It finds which places on Earth are most physically similar to a region on the Moon or Mars, and it explains the results clearly. Users choose a region on the Moon or Mars on a 3D globe that we built with CesiumJS. The region can be a point, a rectangle or a polygon that the user draws. The app then turns this region into a feature vector that works the same way for every planet. The vector has 24 numerical features in 8 groups, plus a terrain class. The groups are:

Topography: average slope, slope variation, roughness, local relief, crater/pit density

Surface: albedo, thermal inertia (as a percentile within its own planet), rock abundance

Temperature and light: minimum temperature, day-night temperature difference, time spent below 0 °C, noon sun height

Water and ice: dryness, near-surface ground ice

Mineralogy: olivine, pyroxene, plagioclase, evaporite/sulfate, iron oxide, clay, carbonate

Processes and life: dust activity, vegetation

Underground: caves and lava tubes

Terrain class

We do not use absolute elevation on purpose. Height above a reference surface does not mean the same thing on different planets.

We compare this vector with two things. The first is a list of 16 documented analog sites on Earth that we collected from scientific papers: Kula Volcanic Field, Lake Salda, the McMurdo Dry Valleys, the Atacama Desert, Mauna Kea, Iceland (Laki), the Deccan Traps, Etna, Don Juan Pond, Río Tinto, Salar de Uyuni, the McCartys lava flow, the San Francisco Volcanic Field, Lonar Crater, Dallol and Haughton Crater. The second is a global grid of Earth that we built with Google Earth Engine. It has 58,289 land cells at about 50 km resolution. To compare them, we use a weighted Euclidean (RMS) distance. First, we scale each feature to a fixed physical range. For example, slope goes from 0 to 30° and minimum temperature goes from −240 to 30 °C. This way, slope in degrees and mineral abundance as a ratio can be compared fairly. The ranges come from physics, not from the data, so a site’s score does not change when we add new sites to the catalog. We did not use cosine similarity because it ignores differences in size. The result is a Similarity Index (SI) from 0 to 100. There are four mission profiles (landing, resources, habitat and science), and each profile gives different weights to the groups. Users do not only see something like “this region is 79 points similar to Lake Salda.” They also see which groups add the most to the similarity, where the analogy breaks down (the two values are shown side by side), and how much of the data is available.

The main benefit of the project is that it makes one expensive and risky step of mission planning easier: choosing the right test site on Earth. Today, space agencies test rovers, drilling systems, habitat prototypes and astronaut training at analog sites on Earth. But deciding which site fits which target usually depends on expert experience and on papers spread across many sources. Analog Atlas makes this decision measurable, repeatable and comparable. We first tested our method on matches that scientists already trust. We locked these matches before our first run, and Jezero Crater → Lake Salda is one of them. For four or five of the five targets, the known analog appears in the top 5 results. With random selection, the chance of this is 31%. Jezero → Lake Salda comes first in every profile. Then we used the same method to scan the whole Earth. For example, for Jezero in the science profile, central Afghanistan (SI 79.2, in the top 0.1% of all land cells), the Pamir Mountains in Tajikistan and northern Somalia appear as new candidates that are not on any campaign list. Every result card is linked to its sources.

We want the project to make an impact on four levels. On the scientific level, we want analog site selection to be a data-based decision instead of a choice based on intuition. On the practical level, we want to save time and money in mission planning by reducing expensive fieldwork at the wrong test sites. On the equity level, we want to point out an imbalance. We looked at 41 analog field campaigns. NASA took part in 22 of them, and 19 of those 22 (86%) took place in high-income countries. No space agency has organized a field analog campaign in a low-income country. For this reason, Analog Atlas treats the Global South as a priority, not as a filter. Places with a scientific similarity score above 60 get small bonuses for income group, novelty and access. No place is removed from the list, and the pure similarity score is always shown next to it. On the educational and social level, we want students, teachers and curious people to understand the Moon and Mars through their own planet. When someone chooses Jezero Crater on Mars and compares it with Lake Salda in Türkiye, a faraway planet becomes a real and familiar place. This also has the potential to make Türkiye’s analog sites more visible around the world.

We wrote the interface with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We used CesiumJS for the 3D globe, and the Moon and Mars images come from NASA Trek services (LRO WAC, Viking MDIM 2.1). The similarity calculation runs in the browser inside a Web Worker. In the background, we built a data pipeline with Python: pandas and NumPy for data processing, FastAPI for an optional API and unittest for 36 automated tests. We pulled the global Earth grid from Google Earth Engine. The datasets we used are NASADEM and Copernicus GLO-30 terrain data, MODIS surface temperature, albedo and vegetation, GPM IMERG precipitation, TerraClimate evaporation, MERRA-2 dust and ASTER mineral indicators. We collected the values for the analog sites from published papers and from NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) reports. Our code is open on GitHub, and the website is live on GitHub Pages. The pre-calculated discoveries are built into the page, so the app works in a normal browser without special hardware or a server, even without an internet connection. We chose this on purpose because we want the tool to be usable in schools and by teams with limited resources.

How we used AI. During the hackathon we used Claude (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant, through Claude Code. It worked as a pair programmer and a research helper; it is not part of the product. We used it to:

write and debug code, such as the Web Worker similarity engine, the Python data pipeline and its tests, and the in-browser discovery search for regions that users draw themselves;

organize data, such as the list of 41 analog field campaigns and the site values we took from papers and NTRS reports, and to check the DOIs of our references through Crossref;

review the code for bugs and mismatches, for example by checking that the results in the browser match the results of the Python backend;

write the documentation, draft the presentation text and refine the interface design.

AI is not used in the analysis itself. The Similarity Index is a fixed, open formula. There is no machine-learning model or language model inside Analog Atlas, so the same input always gives the same result, and anyone can recompute it. The team made every decision about the method: the features, the physical ranges, the profile weights, the locked validation pairs and the Global South rules. We read, ran and tested everything the assistant produced, and we checked every source it suggested before we used it. We did not use AI to generate any images. All screenshots come from the running app, and the planetary images come from NASA Trek.

The creative side of our project is that it reverses the usual approach and puts transparency at the center. Analog sites are usually described starting from Earth: “This place on Earth looks like Mars.” We let users start from the target region on the other planet instead. The question changes from “Which analogs do we have?” to “Where is the best analog for this target?” We call this “Anchor & Discover.” First, the method proves that it can find the known analogs correctly. Then it uses the same measure to search the whole Earth for places that have not been used yet. The second new idea is that every result also tells you clearly where the similarity ends. For example, basalts on Earth have never been exposed to space weathering, but on the Moon the same rocks form nanophase iron and agglutinates. So even an analog with a high score cannot replace the target in every way. Showing differences next to similarities stops the tool from giving false confidence.

As a team, we cared most about scientific honesty. First, the Moon and Mars relief in the browser is a seeded fractal model linked to documented control values. We never present it as a measured digital elevation model (DEM), and the interface says this clearly. Second, we gave every value a reliability label: measured, derived or proxy. We clearly state that the mineral indicators in the global grid are rough and not calibrated. We also report our validation results, including the ones that failed. The Gale → Mauna Kea match does not make the top 5 in the science profile. In our locked list of 10 candidates, 3 candidates reach the top 10% most similar places on Earth in the science profile, while the expected number for random points is 1.2. We present this as a moderate signal, not as strong proof. Third, we accept that no analog on Earth is perfect. Gravity, atmospheric density, the radiation environment and day length cannot be copied exactly anywhere on Earth. We do not add these differences to the score, but we show them on every result card. Fourth, we cared about accessibility. Someone who is not an expert can use the tool with a few clicks, and the results are shown both as a number and as a clear explanation. Finally, we paid attention to traceability. We linked every value and every claim to a source, so a judge, a scientist or a student can check where any result comes from.
